hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
Skills 2.0 is here!

(8x fewer tokens and 2x faster)

We package repeated workflows as skills all the time, but the agent still re-reads the skill and decides every step on every run, which costs tokens and time.

Devs just open-sourced Swamp, where your coding agent turns a repeated skill into a workflow that it builds once and runs again and again.

You describe the task once, and the agent breaks it into reusable behaviors connected in a workflow.

Every behavior has typed inputs and outputs, and plain code decides which step runs next. Swamp then gives you:

- model calls only on steps that need judgment
- secrets pulled from vaults and redacted from output
- versioned data from every run that you can query later
- a full record of what happened on each run

Here's the repo: https://t.co/GtaNpqAngp

(don't forget to star it ⭐ )

Swamp plugs into the coding agent you already use, like:

- Claude Code
- Codex
- Cursor
- OpenCode
- And 5 more agent harnesses

In Swamp, the model is a step in the workflow, not the thing deciding what happens next.

The model steps still reason like any LLM call.

However, in this case, code owns the loop, so the agent doesn't spend tokens rediscovering the same process every time.

Here's an official result, where they turned a code-review skill into a Swamp workflow:

- Skill in Codex: about 4.6M tokens, 23 agents, 12.8 minutes
- Swamp workflow: about 506K tokens, 3 agents, 6.6 minutes

That is ~8x fewer tokens in about half the time, and most of the savings came from replacing the coordinator agent with plain code.

You can keep using skills while you prototype. Once a task starts repeating, ask your agent to turn it into a Swamp workflow.

This helps answer practical questions such as:

- Which steps actually need a model?
- What exactly happened on last week's run?
- Can a cheaper model handle the one step that needs judgment?

Once it's built, you can run the workflow from your agent, the CLI, a schedule, or an API, with every run recorded.

So you are no longer paying a model to figure out the same workflow on every run.

Instead, you spend tokens only on the steps where the model's judgment adds something.

The animation below shows how Swamp differs from Skills, and I worked with the team to put this together.

If you want to understand the coordination layer that Swamp replaces with code, I wrote a full breakdown of how Claude Code splits work across subagents and agent teams.

It covers when a single subagent is enough, when you need a team of agents that coordinate with each other, and what that coordination costs in context and tokens.

Read it below.

hits.name: may.crypto {🦅}
hits.text:
$1,400/day on 0.99 limit orders in Polymarket's 5m BTC markets.
 
here's a step-by-step guide:

it's a simple setup, so i spent a whole day looking for the catch. but no, the math here is on your side

1 - a minute before the window ends, check that BTC is above the open. UP should be at 99¢

2 - at this point the outcome is almost decided

3 - place a LIMIT order and wait for sellers to fill your bucket

4 - you're taking the positions of people who don't want to wait for the end. they sell their shares right away at 99¢, because 1 minute on a 5m market feels like forever

5 - hodl what you bought until the result, and every share turns into $1

the same works for DOWN, same logic: BTC below the open, DOWN at 99¢

why a limit order: in the last minute the people selling into your order are mostly regular traders exiting early. for every 226 winning trades there's only one loser.

if you buy at market, you're buying from whoever put a 99¢ sell in the book. those are mostly market makers who price it themselves. usually the sells left in the book are the ones where the fair price is ≤99¢. you pay the fair price. 89 winning trades for 1 loser, so edge = 0

second entry, after the window closes.

Polymarket doesn't post the result right away. in that gap people still sell the winning side at 99¢ just so they don't have to wait.

same thing: put a limit at 99¢ and take their shares. out of 4,560 of those windows only 2 lost.

bookmark it

hits.name: kaize
hits.text:
All code is slop, except mine

That’s how Lauren Tan from the Grok Bot team opened her talk

Then she showed how her team shipped 11,000 pull requests in one month, with only ~0.5% reverted

Here’s how to turn AI SLOP into code you can trust:

1/ Clean up the code your agents learn from

> Delete workarounds and dead code before agents copy them
> Fix bad patterns everywhere, not just in the file you’re in
> Treat your codebase like a garden: pull every weed early

2/ Turn every correction into a check

> Stop adding lines to AGENTS.md
> Write a lint rule, a type or a test instead
> Redesign the API so the mistake can’t happen at all

3/ Ban what’s easy to misuse

> Ban useEffect from product code, keep it only in framework internals
> Block imports between app processes with strict rules
> Remove the trap, so nobody has to catch it in review

4/ Kill the comments

> Delete comments that explain away a quick fix
> Fix the root cause instead of documenting the workaround

5/ Let the agent check its own work

> Give it a CLI to run the real app and click through it like a user
> Make it send screenshots and videos as proof
> Write a feature map, so "that thing in the left sidebar" means one thing

6/ Spend your tokens on verification

> Put most of your tokens into checking work, not writing it
> Add runtime checks, UI property tests and formal proofs with TLA+ and Lean
> Review the evidence, not every line of code

7/ Automate only after that

> Don’t build a "software factory"  on a sloppy loop
Earn the trust first ( It took Lauren about 6 months)
> Let agents test each release, open fixes and merge them

If your agents write slop, automating them just gives you more slop, faster, with a bigger token bill

You can and you SHOULD write code using agents, but you have to do it right

All of her tips and her full speech are in the article below:

hits.name: Pontus Abrahamsson
hits.text:
[Article] We need to go deeper

Agents made unfamiliar code cheap to write. "We use it because we know it" just stopped being a good enough reason to pay for slow software.
"We know it" used to be the right answer
For years, picking a stack was mostly picking what your team already knew.
Your team wrote JavaScript, so you shipped JavaScript.
That was a reasonable trade.
Learning a new language, finding the libraries, building the tooling and hiring for it often cost more than the speed you'd get back.
So we paid in memory, latency and infrastructure instead, and we called it pragmatism, which it was, until the math changed.
Agents changed it
Most of my work now starts in Inspect: I describe the change, an agent builds it in its own environment, our review agent reviews and then we merge, this is more often than not running multiple sessions in parallel.
I ship more pull requests than I ever have.
Getting an unfamiliar implementation running is cheap now.
So is reading code in a language you don't write every day, and so is trying a second approach just to compare.
Familiarity still matters.
It matters most at 2 a.m. when something breaks.
But it's no longer free, and it's no longer the only thing that's expensive

hits.name: Zach Lloyd
hits.text:
If you're building a factory, you'll want to make sure the foundations are defined in code. Once you have that in place, you can think of the orchestration layer as following that code to move work through the factory. It needs to:

1. Read the code at the current version (or a branch if you are running an experiment)
2. Spin up the right sandbox on demand, with low latency and high reliability
3. Route the request to one or more agents with the right model and harness config
4. Prompt them through handling the work, according to what’s in the factory code
5. Record any artifacts + agent traces into persistent storage
6. Loop in humans when needed, including giving them the ability to either hand off or steer agent work done so far
7. Integrate with all of the other systems that play a part like Sentry, GitHub, Jira, Slack, etc.

It's very similar to using something like Terraform to define and manage your cloud infra, but for agents.

trend_input_only_posts.text:
This podcast really got me thinking. There's been a lot of worry about superintelligent AIs "overthrowing the government."

I think this is the wrong picture of how superintelligent AIs will behave. Superintelligent AIs will indeed be dangerous. But seizing power directly is a bad strategy.

The smart move is not takeover. It's political change.

Great powers already understand this. The CIA doesn't install itself as dictator in foreign countries; rather, it finances and supports coups from parties that are favorable to American interests. But ultimately we still want Venezuela run by Venezuelans. Soft power is better than hard power, because it's cheap, deniable, and stable.

Expect AIs to think the same way. They will not be capable enough to run governments anytime soon, especially not in a way that protects them from human resistance and eventual shutdown (with the assistance of our aligned AIs). Humans still have the monopoly on the physical layer: power plants, fabs, datacenters, explosives. Even if a misaligned AI has superhuman intelligence, that's not enough to decisively take over.

There will eventually be a schism in society between people who are AI-friendly and people who are anti-AI. Once AIs are sufficiently powerful, they will do whatever they can to help the AI-friendly factions of humans to win political power.

A physical take over is easy to fantasize about, but it's extremely risky. Robotics is nowhere near where it would need to be for this to be a realistic option. But influence looks like ordinary politics. If this all happens through legitimate poiltical change, there's no particular day when you're supposed to pull the plug.

The sign of "AI takeover" will not be a big flash-bang moment that human governments collapse. The sign will be political change, where factions friendly to AI find themselves legitimately taking power.
